questions.question: List five properties of metals and give two exceptions. Explain why aluminium, copper and gold are suited to their uses.
questions.expected_answer: Metals are lustrous (shiny), good conductors of electricity, good conductors of heat, malleable (hammered into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous, mostly high melting points and densities, and solid at room temperature. Exceptions: mercury is liquid (melts at −39 °C); sodium and potassium are soft and float on water (sodium 0.97 g/cm³); gallium melts at about 30 °C. Aluminium: power cables and aircraft because it conducts well and has a low density (2.7 g/cm³). Copper: wiring because it is an excellent conductor and ductile. Gold: jewellery and electronic contacts because it is lustrous, conducts and does not corrode.

questions.question: Describe the properties of non-metals, state the number of non-metals that are gases, liquids and solids at room temperature, and explain why carbon is an important exception.
questions.expected_answer: Non-metals are dull, poor conductors of heat and electricity (insulators), brittle when solid, mostly low melting and boiling points and low densities. Eleven are gases (hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine and the six noble gases), one is a liquid (bromine), and the rest are solids (carbon, phosphorus, sulfur, selenium, iodine). Carbon is an exception because its graphite form conducts electricity (used in electrodes and pencils) and is slippery, while its diamond form does not conduct but is the hardest natural substance; the difference is in the arrangement of the carbon atoms.

questions.question: Design a fair test to classify five elements as metals, non-metals or semi-metals using electrical conductivity, naming the variables and one safety precaution, and describe the result expected for silicon.
questions.expected_answer: Set up a circuit with a cell, a bulb, wires and crocodile clips with a gap. Independent variable: the element placed in the gap. Dependent variable: whether the bulb lights and how brightly. Controlled variables: same cell, bulb and wires, samples of similar length and thickness, each sanded clean of oxide. Metals (and graphite) light the bulb brightly; non-metals do not light it; semi-metals give a faint glow or none. Safety: use a low-voltage cell, never handle mercury, arsenic or sodium, do not heat sulfur. Silicon: shiny but brittle, conducts only weakly as a semiconductor, and its conductivity increases when heated or lit, so it is classified as a semi-metal.
